messages.mes:
The road took him down between hedged fields, and the walls of Glassmere grew as he walked—grey stone, older than anything he had known, patched in places with newer masonry the color of old bread. Carts and foot traffic thickened near the gate. A drover cursed a stubborn ox in a flat country accent; two students in matching dark blue hoods argued over a slate, one gesturing as if sketching runes in the air.

The gate guards barely looked at travelers. One collected a copper from a carter ahead, waved a woman with geese through, and when Alaric's turn came the guard glanced at the staff slung at his side, at the plain light robes beneath his travel cloak, and jerked his thumb inward without a word. No toll for a man on foot.

Inside, the morning had its full voice on. Smoke from bread ovens, wet cobbles, hemp and tar from a cart of rope being hauled through the crowd. A street of smiths rang away to the left; somewhere a crier was reading out a notice in a bored drone. People in scholar's dress were as common here as farmers—a city that lived partly off its colleges, from the look of it, though the butcher's stall and the knacker's yard went on as ordinary trades do everywhere.

The Guild hall was not hard to find. A wooden sign with the crossed sword-and-quill mark hung over a wide door on a street corner near the market square, and a steady trickle of armed men and women came and went through it. A pair of leather-armored rangers came out arguing about rates; a scarred woman went in with a bundle of something wrapped in oilcloth under one arm.

The hall inside was broad and timbered, lit by high windows. A long counter ran along the right wall, behind it a bored clerk with ink-stained fingers sorting papers. Ahead, a great notice board stood crowded with contract slips, lightly warded glass over it, a queue of three waiting to be served. A few adventurers sat at trestle tables to the left, one asleep on his arms, two playing at dice with copper stakes.

The morning queue shuffled forward, one step at a time.

The queue had thinned to one ahead of him by the time he reached the counter. The clerk—a narrow man past middle age, ink to the second knuckle—finished stamping something, set it aside, and looked up.

"Registration." Not a question; he'd heard the word half a counter's length away a hundred times. He pulled a fresh form and a blank contract slip toward himself, then laid a small pale stone the size of a plum on the counter between them. It sat dull and quiet.

"Two silver, one time. That covers your entry in the rolls, the measuring, and your slip." He tapped the stone with a fingernail. "Hand on this when we do the reading. It tells us your Power Rank—that's your measured strength, F through S. The Guild writes it down, we don't grant it. Your Guild Rank is separate. Everyone starts at Novice, and you climb it by completing contracts, not by killing things in ditches."

He dipped a quill and waited, the form square in front of him.

"Name as you want it in the rolls. Age if you'll give it—optional, but some clients ask. Then the two silver, and we'll do the reading."

Behind, the dice game rattled on. The sleeping man snored. The clerk's quill hung over the paper, and his eyes stayed on Alaric, patient and unhurried.

"Alaric Red. Eighteen." The quill scratched both down in a tight hand. Two silver followed, and the clerk slid them off the counter with a sweep of his thumb, bit one out of old habit, and dropped both into a lockbox under the ledger.

"Hand on the stone."

Alaric laid his palm on it. For a breath nothing happened; then the pale surface warmed under his skin and a dull amber light stirred inside it, slow as honey, settling into a faint steady glow that did not brighten. The clerk watched it, nodded once, and wrote a single letter on the form.

"F." He said it without judgment, the way a man reads a weight off a scale. "Lowest band, where everyone starts. Some stay there their whole lives and eat fine. Don't let it trouble you." He dipped the quill again, finished the last line, and dusted the form with sand before setting it aside.

From a drawer beneath the counter he took a wooden plate the size of a palm, stamped with the crossed sword-and-quill in black ink, and a strip of leather to hang it by. He pushed it across.

"Your Guild plate. Novice rank, first year. It names you in the rolls at any branch—if you lose it, replacing it costs you, so don't. Contracts are taken and closed at this counter or any other. Board's there." He tilted his ink-stained hand toward the great notice board under its warded glass, where paper slips fluttered faintly whenever someone brushed past. "Read what a job asks before you sign for it. Desk closes contracts, not clients, not you. Anything else, ask the duty clerk."

Behind Alaric the queue had grown by two. The clerk's eyes went past his shoulder, already finding the next face.

The slip came off its pin with a small tug of paper. Back at the counter, the man ahead was counting coppers onto the wood while the clerk checked them against a line in his ledger; when the last coin slid into the lockbox, the clerk looked up.

Alaric laid the notice down.

The clerk read it, opened the ledger to a fresh page, and wrote in small even letters: the name, the contract, the day. Then he drew the slip back, set the Guild's stamp to it, and the crossed sword-and-quill sank into the paper with a faint warmth, the black of it settling deeper than ink had any right to.

"Glimmerdeep, level one." He recited it the way a man reads back an order at a chandler's. "Crystal beetles and mineral slimes in the outer galleries — the Argent Veil wants them gone before they let students back in. The cleft's north of the city, where the stream runs out of the hills. A morning's walk on the north road. Academy people hold the entrance; show them your plate and they'll point you in. Anything you kill is yours, and the loose crystal you can pick free. Past the lantern lines is theirs — the deep galleries — so stay this side of them." He turned the slip around and slid it back. "When the level's clear, bring this to any Guild desk and we close it. One hundred twenty copper, from this counter and no other."

The paper was warm under the seal. Behind Alaric, the next in the queue stepped up with a limp and a rolled sleeve, and the clerk drew the ledger toward himself again.

messages.mes:
The north road took him out through the gate with the morning traffic — carts of early vegetables, a drover's dogs, two women walking with hoes over their shoulders — and then the city fell behind and the road narrowed to packed earth between hedgerows.

The hills came up slowly. Past the last farmsteads the hedges gave out and the land turned to grass and grey stone, and the stream he'd been told of ran beside the road, clear over pebbles, running the wrong way for a companion — out of the hills, toward the city. An hour in, his calves knew the climb had begun. Another hour, and the road thinned to a cart track, then to a footpath that followed the water up between shoulders of rock laced with wildflowers.

He smelled the cleft before he saw it: a cool breath from the hills, mineral and faintly sweet, like wet slate and something floral underneath.

The stream ran straight out of the rock face. The cleft itself stood a bowshot above the waterline — a tall jagged mouth in the hillside, and from its edges, crystal. Veins of it ran through the stone like frozen lightning, catching the midday sun and throwing it back in slivers of pale blue and white.

Between the mouth of the cleft and the path stood the academy's mark: wooden survey stakes in a line, lanterns hung on iron hooks — unlit at this hour — and a canvas shelter where two people sat. An older man with a grey beard braided into two short plaits, a counting board across his knees, and a younger woman in academy grey with her boots off, rubbing a foot and arguing at him in a low voice about something written on her slate.

A third figure, arms bare to the shoulder, was hauling a crate up the path from the stream, and it was he who saw Alaric first.

"Company," he called, and set the crate down.

The bearded man looked up from his counting board, eyes going at once to the wooden plate at Alaric's chest.

"Guild work, then. Good." His voice had the dry patience of a man who talked to students all day. "I'm Master Hulric; I keep the tally for the Argent Veil out here. The woman with the slate leaned around him. "The lantern lines mark what's ours. Anything past the third line is the deep galleries and you don't want to be there with a wooden plate, no offense."

"None taken, I'm sure," Hulric said. He nodded toward the cleft mouth, where the crystal veins caught the sun. "The gate-warden will log you in — that's Tamsin, at the mouth. "Kill what you kill, take what crystal you can pick free, and mind the floor under the blue light — the beetles like to freeze still and let you walk to them."

The labourer had drifted closer, wiping his hands on his thighs, and now tilted his head at the cleft with something like sympathy. "Slimes are slow. Beetles aren't," he said, and went back to his crate.

Up at the mouth of the cleft, half in its shadow, a stocky figure in academy grey sat on a stool beside a small table — a ledger open, an inkpot weighted with a chunk of raw crystal. Tamsin, presumably. She hadn't turned around yet; the wind off the stream carried the smell of wet stone and that faint floral sweetness out past her, and somewhere inside the rock, faint and rhythmic, water was dripping onto crystal.

The path up to the gate-warden's table was open.

messages.mes:
Tamsin dipped her pen once more and made a mark in the ledger without looking up.

The cleft mouth swallowed the midday sun within a dozen paces. The crystal in the walls had its own light here — a pale blue glow seeping out of the veins, enough to walk by — and the air turned cold and damp against his skin, tasting of stone and that faint sweetness, stronger now, like crushed flowers over wet rock.

Water dripped somewhere ahead, each drop ringing off crystal and holding its note a moment before the next one. The floor was smooth-worn stone, polished in places to a slick sheen, and old lantern hooks studded the walls at intervals — the first ones empty, then a lit stub guttering in a niche, then another. The academy's lines, still burning from yesterday.

The passage widened and narrowed as it went. Old chisel marks showed where surveyors had cleared fallen rock; a survey stake stood leaning against a wall where something had knocked it over, its ribbon faded. Once, a soft shifting sound off to the left stopped him for a breath — nothing came of it, only a trickle of water finding a new channel.

Past the third lantern line the blue glow thickened. The veins ran broader here, brighter, throwing his shadow long and doubled along the walls, and the floor under that light lay utterly still — no scuttling, no movement, the stillness Hulric and Tamsin had both warned him of.

He backed off the shard-strewn floor to the gallery's edge, where the crystal vein wall rose rough and dry, and lowered himself against it with his staff across his knees.

The thigh had closed to a scabbed line, the calf to two of them, stiff but whole. The ache in his mana channels had eased too, that drained hollow feeling behind his eyes gone quiet.

He rolled his shoulders, worked his boots against the stone, and stood. Blood had dried stiff down his trouser leg and inside the boot, cracking as he moved. messages.mes:
The bolt of pale arcane force leapt from his staff across the short gap and struck the nearer slime square in its milky flank. The body shuddered, crystals inside grinding hard, and the whole mass sagged inward, its surface dimming from wet stone to dead mineral. It slumped apart into a shallow puddle studded with loose crystal shards, and was still.

The second slime woke.

It came fast for something that looked like set jelly — a rippling, dragging surge over the stone, closing the last few paces before he could shift his footing. Its front bulged, stretched, and pressed itself against his boot and shin with a cold, wet weight. Where it touched, his trouser leg hissed faintly and the skin beneath burned — a sharp, chemical sting crawling up his calf, leather going stiff and pale where the thing clung.

He tore his leg free and staggered back a step. The slime rippled after him, a slow grinding pulse, its surface flecked now with threads of dissolved leather. It sat between him and the tunnel wall, close enough to strike, its body quivering with what might have been appetite.

The lance of fire left his staff with a hiss and a bloom of orange light that threw the whole gallery into flickering contrast. It struck the pursuing slime dead center and burst through it, heat flashing the moisture on its surface to steam. The body convolved once, crystals inside cracking like ice in warm water, then collapsed outward into a spreading puddle of wet grit and dissolved mineral. Threads of steam curled off the stain, and the crystal vein's blue glow settled back over the quiet.

Then nothing but the drip of water and his own breathing. His calf still stung where the thing had clung to him, the leather of his trouser leg stiffened and bleached pale.

Three lumps of pale gel and a small milky crystal core sat among the remains — the residue the slimes had left, already settled into his pack's pouch with the rest of the morning's takings. He stood alone in the outer gallery, both shapes now gone, the tunnel ahead of him dark and quiet.
